headline: Pilbara Minerals gets hammered 7.4% as lithium pressures mount, while the Houthis seize the Strait of Hormuz and OpenAI drops GPT-6 Astra.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara copped a heavy 7.4% fall today — its biggest single-day drop in recent memory. Lithium carbonate prices remain under pressure globally as supply continues to outpace demand, and broader commodity sell-offs (tied to Middle East tension and a softening AUD) weighed on the sector. The long-run lithium story is still intact, but the near-term is genuinely rough.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two bounced 2.76% in last night's session despite news that ex-UK Rockstar employees are suing for unfair dismissal. Markets appear to be shaking off the legal noise and refocusing on the GTA VI release hype cycle — that game remains the most anticipated title in years.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google ticked up 0.61% last night in a broadly soft market — a solid relative performance. No major company-specific news; the AI sector generally held up as investors await further product announcements from the big tech names.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft edged up a modest 0.16% last night. Quiet session for the stock — no major news. The broader NASDAQ slipped, so holding flat is a decent result.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS closed up slightly today, broadly tracking last night's US market moves which were mixed. A small positive close in a down ASX session is a reasonable outcome for this ETF.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI dipped a slight 0.37% today on the ASX. No specific catalyst — the AI ETF is broadly tracking the tech sector's cautious tone amid geopolitical uncertainty. Still well down from its highs overall (-13.96% since your purchase).

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG slipped 0.45% today alongside a weak ASX session overall (the ASX 200 fell 0.89%). This is normal noise for a diversified high-growth ETF — nothing to worry about.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE was flat today at $93.02 — unchanged from yesterday's close. Emerging markets are sitting in a holding pattern amid geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East and ongoing questions about the Chinese economy.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Big drop today — but long-term thesis intact
watch_today.detail: Pilbara fell 7.4% today to $4.52, and is now down 32.9% on your total investment. That's a painful session. But the lithium demand story — driven by EVs and battery storage — hasn't changed. What HAS changed is the short-term supply picture: there's too much lithium hitting the market right now, keeping prices low. If you believe in the 5-10 year EV transition, this is noise, not a reason to bail. Sit tight unless you want to top up at these beaten-down levels.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF down 14% overall — but GPT-6 Astra just launched
watch_today.detail: GXAI is your worst-performing holding overall, down ~14% since purchase. However, today OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra — a new generation of AI that's being positioned as a step-change for workplace intelligence. This is the kind of development that GXAI is designed to capture over the long run. The ETF holds AI-focused companies that should benefit from continued AI adoption. A dip like this in a genuine growth theme is typically a hold — or even a top-up opportunity for long-term investors.

watch_today.title: TTWO: Legal noise around Rockstar — don't read too much into it
watch_today.detail: Former UK Rockstar (GTA VI developer, owned by Take-Two) employees are suing for unfair dismissal. The market largely ignored this last night — TTWO rose 2.76%. For a long-term holder, this kind of employment dispute isn't a reason to sell. The GTA VI release remains the core thesis, and that hasn't changed. You're still down 6.5% overall, but the long-term story is intact.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hikes: More pain coming for mortgages and the ASX
watch_today.detail: Multiple major banks — including CommBank — are now tipping two more RBA rate rises before the end of 2026. Higher rates mean tougher conditions for growth stocks and property. The AUD/USD slipped to 0.7175 today. This is worth watching as a general headwind for your portfolio, particularly for the ASX-listed ETFs like VDHG and VGE.

watch_today.title: Strait of Hormuz crisis: Oil fell but risk is rising fast
watch_today.detail: Iran-backed Houthis are moving to seize control of the Strait of Hormuz — one of the world's most critical shipping lanes. A US sail drone was destroyed at the entrance. If this escalates, oil prices could spike sharply from the current $99.67/barrel. That would be inflationary globally and a headwind for equity markets. Crude actually fell 2.74% last night on demand concerns, but the geopolitical risk picture is deteriorating fast. Keep an eye on this over the coming days.

world.summary: The Middle East is the dominant global story today, with Iran-backed Houthis moving on the Strait of Hormuz, Trump promising $5,000 voter checks ahead of US midterms, and a tense geopolitical backdrop across multiple fronts.

stories.title: Houthis seize control of the Strait of Hormuz — one of the world's busiest shipping lanes
stories.why_it_matters: Iran-backed Houthi forces are sweeping toward sudden control over the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow passage through which about 20% of the world's oil flows. A US unmanned sail drone was destroyed at the strait's entrance today. This is a massive deal: if the Houthis close or seriously disrupt the strait, global oil prices could spike dramatically, shipping costs would soar, and economies worldwide — including Australia's — would feel the inflationary hit. Trump has reportedly said the war will end 'immediately' after the US midterms, but that's cold comfort right now.

stories.title: Iran strikes US jets, Trump says war ends 'immediately' after midterms
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has struck US military aircraft in an escalation of the ongoing Middle East conflict, with CBS News reporting the jets were damaged in strikes. President Trump responded by saying the war will end 'immediately' after November's US midterm elections — implying the conflict is being politically managed. This kind of geopolitical brinkmanship creates real uncertainty for global markets, oil prices, and trade routes. If Trump does pull back post-midterms, it could bring a sharp de-escalation — but a lot can happen between now and then.

stories.title: Trump promises $5,000 checks to Americans if Republicans win the midterms
stories.why_it_matters: Trump is promising $5,000 cash payments to every American if the Republican Party wins November's midterm elections. The New York Times estimates the cost at more than $1 trillion. Economists are sceptical: trillion-dollar cash handouts without corresponding revenue would balloon the US deficit and could be highly inflationary — meaning the US Federal Reserve would likely need to keep interest rates higher for longer. That's bad news for global growth stocks and could put pressure on the AUD. Worth watching as the midterms approach.

stories.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow voter-screening tool — DOJ demands voter data after 23 court losses
stories.source: The New York Times / The Independent
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration has gone to the Supreme Court seeking approval for a voter-screening tool, even as the DOJ is separately demanding that election officials hand over voter data — despite losing 23 prior legal battles on this exact issue. Critics say this is an attempt to build a centralised database to challenge voter eligibility en masse. With midterms approaching, the fight over who gets to vote is heating up significantly in the US, with potential implications for the election outcome and — by extension — global markets and trade policy.

stories.title: Global coal demand set for new record as Middle East conflict disrupts energy markets
stories.why_it_matters: The International Energy Agency (IEA) says global coal demand is on track for a new record in 2026, driven in part by the Middle East conflict disrupting oil and gas supplies. Countries are scrambling for alternative energy sources. For Australia, this is a mixed signal: our coal exporters benefit from higher demand and prices, but it also signals a delay in the global clean-energy transition that underpins the long-term lithium/EV investment thesis.

markets.summary: A broadly negative session on both sides of the Pacific. The ASX 200 fell 0.89% today as Middle East tensions, commodity weakness, and RBA rate-hike fears weighed on sentiment. Last night on Wall Street, the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both slipped, though individual tech stocks held up reasonably well. Oil dropped sharply on demand fears despite the Hormuz crisis. Gold was essentially flat. The Aussie dollar weakened against the USD.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: ASX fell 0.89% today — broad-based weakness driven by rate hike expectations and commodity sector pressure.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: The S&P 500 slipped 0.58% last night — cautious sentiment amid Middle East escalation and US political noise.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: NASDAQ fell 0.65% last night despite most big tech names holding steady — broader growth stock nervousness.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil fell 2.74% last night — the market is pricing in demand destruction fears despite the very real Hormuz risk. Watch this one closely.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold barely moved — staying near record highs as a safe haven amid geopolitical uncertainty.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar slipped 0.63% as RBA rate hike bets and a risk-off global mood weighed on it.

politics.summary: Australian interest rate news dominated the domestic agenda today, with multiple major banks now tipping two more RBA rate hikes before the end of 2026 — bad news for mortgage holders and growth-oriented investors.

stories.title: CommBank and other major lenders tip two more RBA rate hikes before end of 2026
stories.why_it_matters: CommBank's economics team is now forecasting two further RBA interest rate rises before the end of 2026 — meaning Australian mortgage holders could be paying even more by Christmas. The bank's report, titled 'Higher rates, harder choices', argues that sticky inflation and a resilient labour market are giving the RBA little reason to pause. For everyday Aussies with a home loan, each 0.25% rate rise adds roughly $80/month to a $500,000 mortgage. For investors, higher rates tend to hurt growth stocks and put downward pressure on property values.

stories.title: AUD holds firm as RBA rate hike bets rise ahead of US inflation data
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian dollar has been caught between two forces: rising RBA rate hike expectations (which would normally push the AUD higher) and a global risk-off mood from the Middle East crisis (which pushes it lower). Today the AUD slipped to 0.7175 US cents. US CPI (inflation) data is due soon — if it comes in hot, the US Fed may keep rates elevated, which tends to strengthen the USD and weaken the AUD further. A lower AUD means your US-listed holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO) are worth more in Australian dollar terms when converted — a small silver lining.

ai.summary: The biggest AI story today is the release of GPT-6 Astra from OpenAI — billed as a new generation of intelligence for both general use and the workplace. Alongside that, AI regulation is front and centre globally, from Australia to the EU to the UK.

stories.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Astra — a new generation of AI intelligence
stories.why_it_matters: OpenAI has officially released GPT-6 Astra today — the successor to GPT-4 and GPT-4o. It's being positioned as a step-change in AI capability, with a specific 'for work' variant targeting enterprise and professional use cases. While the full technical details are still emerging, this is significant for anyone using AI tools at work — expect smarter assistants, better reasoning, and more autonomous task-handling. It's also directly relevant to your GXAI.AX holding, which invests in companies across the AI value chain.

stories.title: US agencies accuse six Chinese AI firms of stealing training data from Claude, GPT, Gemini and Grok
stories.why_it_matters: US government agencies have accused six Chinese AI companies of systematically scraping and using training data from Western AI models — including OpenAI's Claude, Google's Gemini, xAI's Grok, and others. If proven, this would represent a major form of intellectual property theft, essentially letting Chinese firms fast-track their AI development by piggy-backing on billions of dollars of Western R&D. This is likely to accelerate the AI cold war between the US and China — and could trigger export controls or sanctions that affect global tech supply chains.

stories.title: Australia's AI regulation framework: what it means for businesses
stories.why_it_matters: Australia is developing its own AI regulatory framework and iTWire is reporting today on what this means practically for companies — specifically how it affects their risk management. In plain terms: Aussie businesses that use AI tools (from chatbots to hiring algorithms) will likely need to document the risks those tools create and show they're managing them. This is early-stage but will increasingly affect how Australian companies adopt and invest in AI — relevant background for your GXAI.AX ETF.

stories.title: EU responds to AI extinction warnings with measured regulatory approach
stories.why_it_matters: The EU is pushing back against doomsday AI warnings from researchers and tech executives, instead opting for a pragmatic regulatory path. Politico reports the EU is focused on the AI Act's implementation — classifying AI systems by risk level and setting rules accordingly — rather than pausing development entirely. For investors, this is broadly positive: it suggests Europe won't kneecap AI development, but will add compliance costs for companies operating there. Relevant to your GXAI.AX holding which has exposure to global AI companies.

sport.summary: NRL Finals Week 1 is underway — the Knights upset the Rabbitohs last night, and there are big team news stories ahead of this weekend's remaining finals games. The AFL trade period is heating up with some significant signings. The US Open tennis is producing notable results.

stories.title: Knights knock out Rabbitohs 20-10 in Finals Week 1 opener
stories.why_it_matters: The Newcastle Knights beat the South Sydney Rabbitohs 20-10 at Allianz Stadium tonight in the first elimination final of the NRL Finals. The Knights advance; the Rabbitohs' season is over. Wayne Bennett's Souths couldn't get it done at home — a tough night for the red and green. The Knights now face a top-four team next week.

stories.title: Finals Late Mail: Sharks lose Puru, Latrell warning for Knights, Cowboys face hurdle
stories.why_it_matters: Heading into Saturday's finals, the Sharks have lost Puru to injury — a blow for Cronulla ahead of their clash with the Cowboys at Allianz Stadium. Wayne Bennett (now coaching the Knights) has issued a warning about Latrell Mitchell's potential impact. The Cowboys are also facing a fitness hurdle with at least one key player racing the clock. Saturday's games are Warriors v Dolphins (4:05pm, Auckland) and Sharks v Cowboys (7:50pm, Sydney).

stories.title: AFL trade season: Jesse Hogan picks Collingwood, Saints re-sign trio, Crows await compensation
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL trade period is producing its first major move: tall forward Jesse Hogan has chosen Collingwood, rejecting what was reportedly a top-3 or top-4 salary offer to do so. St Kilda has re-signed three players to stay, and the Adelaide Crows are awaiting a compensation draft pick. The AFL has also warned clubs about the risks of trading for a currently suspended Sydney Swans player — anyone picking him up will inherit the remaining ban.

stories.title: Australian Open confirms stance on five-set matches for 2027
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian Open has made an official statement on whether the five-set format will remain for the 2027 tournament, amid a broader global tennis debate about changing scoring systems to make matches shorter and more TV-friendly. The AO's position will set a tone for other Grand Slams. With Carlos Alcaraz losing at the US Open quarter-finals this week, and Federer's legacy being revisited, the sport is in a reflective moment about its future direction.
